Name: distractor_hijacked_retrieval
Title: Hijacked Attention: How Salient-but-Irrelevant Context Redirects an LLM's Retrieval Key Away from a Stored Fact
Short Hypothesis: When a query is embedded in context that contains a salient-but-irrelevant entity (a distractor sharing surface features with the true subject), the LLM's retrieval attention is partially 'hijacked': the retrieval key computed at the answer position blends the true subject with the distractor, degrading recall of a fact the model demonstrably stores. We hypothesize that (1) the fraction of answer-position attention diverted to the distractor causally predicts per-example recall failure, (2) these are override/routing failures rather than knowledge gaps (the fact stays decodable in mid layers), and (3) a lightweight 'attention re-focusing' intervention that down-weights the distractor's key/value contribution restores correct recall without weight edits and without hurting distractor-free queries.
Related Work: Prior distraction/robustness work is largely behavioral: 'Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context' (Shi et al. 2023) and long-context 'lost-in-the-middle' (Liu et al. 2023) document degradation but give no mechanistic account. Knowledge-boundary and internal-state work (Ni et al. 2025; Ren et al. 2023) studies when models know vs. don't know but not how irrelevant context reroutes retrieval. Factual-recall circuit work (Geva et al. 2023; Fierro et al. 2024) dissects clean single-fact recall with no distractors. RAG context-vs-parametric conflict work (Yu et al. 2023; Wadhwa et al. 2024) studies conflicting *content*, not attention hijacking by a semantically confusable but content-irrelevant entity. Our contribution is the first mechanistic account tying distractor-induced recall failure to a measurable, causal diversion of answer-position retrieval attention, an example-level diagnostic separating hijacking from knowledge gaps, and a targeted attention-refocusing repair with false-positive controls.
Abstract: Language models often answer a factual question correctly in isolation but fail when the same question is surrounded by salient-but-irrelevant context—a nearby entity that shares surface or semantic features with the true subject. It is unclear whether this reflects lost knowledge or misdirected retrieval. We propose that irrelevant context hijacks retrieval attention: at the answer position the model's retrieval key blends the true subject with the distractor, so the correct fact—still stored—fails to surface. We test three claims on matched queries where a fact is asked cleanly, then re-asked embedded in context containing a controlled distractor entity. First, using logit lens and linear probes we show the correct answer remains decodable in mid layers regardless of the distractor (storage invariance), ruling out knowledge loss. Second, we measure the fraction of answer-position attention diverted from the true subject to the distractor and test whether this diversion causally predicts recall failure (AUROC, incremental over a difficulty baseline), validating causality via attention-knockout that restores the diverted attention. Third, we introduce a training-free 'attention re-focusing' intervention that down-weights the distractor tokens' key/value contribution at the retrieval heads and measure recall recovery, false-intervention rate on distractor-free queries (must not degrade), and hallucination rate on genuinely-unknown facts. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3 across scales, and we test whether hijacking susceptibility and repair efficacy change with scale and distractor type (lexical-overlap vs. same-category vs. same-relation).
Experiments: 1) BENCHMARK: From CounterFact/T-REx, take ~4k facts (subject-relation-answer) the model answers correctly in isolation (verified stored). For each, build a CLEAN query and matched DISTRACTOR variants embedding the query in a short context containing an irrelevant entity of three controlled types: (a) LEXICAL-OVERLAP (name shares tokens/prefix with true subject), (b) SAME-CATEGORY (same entity type, different attribute), (c) SAME-RELATION (a different subject with the same relation but different answer). Distractor sentences are content-irrelevant to the asked fact (they do not assert a conflicting answer), isolating attention hijacking from content conflict. 2) STORAGE INVARIANCE: With logit lens and per-layer linear probes at the subject/answer position, test whether the correct answer stays decodable in mid layers across clean and distractor variants; report cross-condition probe AUROC. Prediction: high storage invariance (failures are not knowledge loss). 3) ATTENTION-DIVERSION MEASUREMENT: At the answer position, for each retrieval head (identified via clean-query activation patching as those transporting the fact), compute the fraction of attention mass on true-subject tokens vs. distractor tokens; define DiversionScore = distractor mass / (subject + distractor mass), aggregated over retrieval heads. 4) PREDICTIVE TEST: Test whether DiversionScore predicts per-example recall failure; report AUROC and incremental AUROC over a difficulty-only baseline (answer frequency, isolated logit margin, context length). Compare across distractor types (prediction: lexical-overlap most hijacking). 5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: For hijacked-error cases, use attention-knockout to zero the answer-position attention to distractor tokens (redistributing to subject) and measure whether the correct answer is restored; compare to knocking out a random non-distractor token as control. Also patch the clean-query answer-position residual into the distractor run to confirm the fact would surface. 6) ATTENTION RE-FOCUSING INTERVENTION: Training-free—at the identified retrieval heads, down-weight (scale by beta<1) the key/value contribution of distractor-span tokens at the answer position before softmax renormalization. Measure RECOVERY RATE on hijacked errors, FALSE-INTERVENTION rate on distractor-free queries (must not degrade), HALLUCINATION rate on genuinely-unknown facts (must not fabricate), and SIDE EFFECTS on unrelated correctly-answered queries. Baselines: no intervention, explicit prompt instruction to ignore irrelevant context, CoT, and random-span down-weighting control (to attribute gains to targeting the distractor, not generic attention perturbation). Note: distractor span is available in our controlled benchmark; we frame this as a mechanistic probe of hijacking and also test an unsupervised variant that flags high-attention non-subject spans automatically. 7) SCALING/GENERALIZATION: Repeat on Pythia (410M/1.4B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B); report whether DiversionScore predictiveness, hijacking rate by distractor type, and repair efficacy change with scale, and whether retrieval-head sets and the down-weighting recipe transfer across relations. METRICS: cross-condition storage-probe AUROC, DiversionScore predictive & incremental AUROC, causal restoration rate, recovery/false-intervention/hallucination/side-effect rates, distractor-type effect sizes, scaling trends.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Mid-layer decodability may overstate 'storage'; we require causal patching corroboration (clean-residual patching restores the answer) and treat decodability as necessary-not-sufficient. 2) DiversionScore may correlate with generic difficulty or context length; we control via incremental AUROC over a difficulty+length baseline and matched-length distractor-free controls. 3) Retrieval-head identification is imperfect and heads may be polysemantic; we aggregate over a head set and report robustness to head-set size. 4) The re-focusing intervention risks harming cases where the 'distractor' is actually relevant; our benchmark guarantees content-irrelevance, and false-intervention/side-effect rates are explicit success criteria; the unsupervised variant is reported separately as a harder test. 5) Some distractor failures may reflect genuine ambiguity resolution rather than hijacking; the SAME-RELATION type partially probes this and we analyze error types separately. 6) Effects may be architecture-specific (GQA vs MHA changes head structure); we characterize across families rather than assume universality. 7) Automatic distractor-span detection in the unsupervised variant may misfire on real irrelevant context of varied form; we report its precision/recall against the controlled ground truth.
